analysis.one_liner: Bans insurers from using credit scores to set auto insurance rates.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Financial Services Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Insurers in most states use a driver's credit history to decide whether to sell them auto insurance and how much to charge, on the theory that credit predicts claims. This bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act to make it illegal for anyone to use a credit report, credit score, or any similar score in underwriting or pricing personal auto insurance. It leaves in place two other tools insurers use: accident and claims-history databases, and state motor vehicle records of accidents and moving violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers whose credit is weak or thin — often younger people, people with low incomes, people who went through a job loss, medical bills, or divorce — who today pay more, or can be refused coverage, because of their credit. All drivers who want rates based on driving rather than finances also benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers with poor or thin credit

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits furnishing or using any consumer report, credit score, or similar predictor in underwriting or rating personal auto insurance [S3].
Preserves claims-history databases like CLUE and A-PLUS, and state motor vehicle driving records, so insurers can still price on actual driving and loss history [S3].
Carves out only personal automobile lines as defined by the NAIC's coding matrix, leaving other insurance products untouched [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Auto insurers would lose a pricing tool they credit with improving risk accuracy, and credit bureaus and scoring companies would lose the auto-insurance share of their business. Some drivers with strong credit could see rates move up if insurers rebalance toward driving-based factors.

drawbacks.text: Insurers and regulators in many states say credit-based insurance scores are a statistically strong predictor of claims, so barring them could raise prices for drivers with strong credit who currently pay less [S3].
The bill is a flat ban with no transition period, so insurers would have to rebuild rating plans around the remaining driving and loss-history factors on short notice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: removing credit from pricing protects drivers whose finances have gone badly, at the possible expense of drivers with strong credit. Since the bill keeps claims-history and driving-record databases, insurers would retain direct measures of driving, which is the case for treating the swap as a fairness improvement rather than a loss of information. The lack of a transition mechanism is a design weakness but a modest one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Introduced on March 14, 2019 by Rep. Rashida Tlaib with 25 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
Referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, the committee with jurisdiction over the Fair Credit Reporting Act [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no markup, no report, no floor vote. The bill gathered 26 cosponsors over the Congress, all Democrats [S4].
The measure died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021, without ever reaching the House floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Auto insurers and credit-scoring companies are better off, because they kept the ability to price and underwrite auto coverage using credit. Drivers with poor credit, who would have paid less under the ban, gained nothing.

for.name: Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the push to ban credit-based auto insurance pricing.

for.name: 26 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Reps. Debbie Dingell, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ayanna Pressley, and Pramila Jayapal.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the Fair Credit Reporting Act
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee on introduction and never scheduled a markup or floor action; the bill sat for 22 months until the Congress ended.

against.name: Property-casualty insurance industry
against.role: Auto insurers that use credit-based insurance scores in pricing
against.what_they_did: Defended credit-based pricing as an accurate risk predictor and opposed state and federal bans on its use.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 26 cosponsors were Democrats, no Republican signed on, and the all-Democratic Financial Services Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill removes credit scores from underwriting and rating, a tool insurers use to charge drivers with weak credit more. Insurers' financial interest runs against drivers with poor credit, though some well-credited drivers might pay slightly more.
Companies like the consumer reporting agencies sell credit reports and specially built insurance scores to insurers for auto underwriting; the bill eliminates that market for auto insurance.
